newsitem.title: INDIA: Hong Kong handover casts China's shadow on India.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong handover casts China's shadow on India.

text.p: Sino-Indian relations could be further strained if China uses Hong Kong's economic might to bolster its military strength, Indian defence analysts say.
Analysts said Hong Kong's July 1 return to Beijing added power to China's economic muscle. This will strengthen its formidable military might, which India has been wary of for decades, they said.

"The handover marks not only the end of colonialism, it also heralds the pre-eminence of China in Asia, and all the Asian countries will have to accommodate this reality," security affairs analyst C. Rajamohan told Reuters.
"We have an edge on the conventional weapons side over China, but this will change as they have a lot more resources now," he said.
Ties between the two ancient civilisations, which together hold about one third of the world's people, have been strained since a war in 1962 over their snow-laden Himalayan border.
Indian analysts say China's first nuclear test two years after the war prompted India's only atomic explosion in 1974.

"Hong Kong's return to China will increase China's assertiveness in Asia and international affairs. This can only unnerve China's neighbours," said Brahma Chellaney, strategic studies analyst at the Centre for Policy Research.
"We are not at all prepared for meeting the challenge of China, and the challenge is likely to grow significantly in the years to come," Chellaney said.

China is one of the world's five declared nuclear powers, and western intelligence officials say they will be watching to see whether it uses the former British colony to start military-related businesses.
India says it has no nuclear arms, but experts say it can swiftly assemble them.

Rajamohan said India's entry last year into the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) Regional Forum indicated that other, smaller countries in the region were happy to help it emerge as an Asian counterweight to the Chinese giant.
The analysts said India would need to focus on economic growth before even thinking of matching the military power of China, which spans a wide Asian frontier from Afghanistan to North Korea.
But New Delhi must also develop a credible nuclear deterrent and a reliable missile delivery system to ward off threats from both China and India's 50-year arch rival, Pakistan, they said.

"Indian policy-makers will sooner or later have to confront the Chinese challenge by having an overt nuclear posture and by developing long-range missiles that can reach the heart of China," Chellaney said.
India's 2,500-km (1,500-mile) Agni missile is regarded as a potential deterrent to China while its medium-range Prithvi is considered more suited as a deterrent against Pakistan.
A parliamentary panel recommended in April that India quickly build the Agni. But the country's shrinking defence budget has raised question marks over its missile programme.

The Agni project was mothballed last year due to what defence analysts said was U.S.-led opposition to India's missile programme. Washington says the programme could fuel a destabilising arms race in South Asia.
"The United States is building up China as a second power in a bipolar world," said defence analyst K. Subrahmanyam.

"If India expands its trade with the U.S. to something like $100 billion annually, the U.S. will not put pressure on India on the nuclear or missile issues," he said, referring to Washington's reluctance to penalise China for reported arms transfers to Pakistan. Indo-U.S. trade is now at $9.5 billion.

"If you have the nuclear and missile capability to deter China, and can grow economically and enlarge trade with the United States, the European Union and Japan, it is a way of balancing growing Chinese power," Subrahmanyam said.
To deal with China, India would need to focus less on troubles with its smaller neighbours, Rajamohan said.
"We need to get out of the quagmire of South Asian diplomacy, but first we have to sort out the pygmies who are trying to tire us out," he added.
Neighbouring Pakistan, which has fought three wars with India, is also considered a "nuclear threshold" state.
A decades-old military relationship between China and Pakistan, which says it has achieved nuclear capability without conducting a single test, has often stoked regional tensions.

Both Pakistan and China have denied Western reports that Beijing transferred to Islamabad nuclear weapons components and Chinese missiles that can deliver nuclear warheads. But India, wedged between the two countries, views their close ties with much concern.
